The primary objective is to minimize the phase dispersion among the oscillators at the moment of activation. Mathematically, this is expressed as minimizing the variance of the onset times across the five interior linemen. If we denote the reaction time of the $i$-th lineman as $\tau_i$, the collective efficiency is inversely proportional to $\text{Var}(\tau)$. The 'starting signal' acts as a Dirac delta function in the temporal domain, triggering a simultaneous state transition from rest to kinetic engagement.

Following the temporal synchronization, the system transitions into the spatial assignment regime. Here, the dualities emerge between the offensive and defensive topologies. The offensive line seeks to maximize the volume of the protected pocket (a convex hull optimization), while the defensive line aims to minimize it by applying maximal shear forces at weak points in the adjacency matrix. The 'breaking through' simulation represents a stress test of this topological integrity. Failure modes manifest when the temporal synchronization breaks down (false starts or slow reactions), which immediately degrades the spatial assignment kernel, allowing the defensive operators to exploit the resulting phase gaps. The rigorous practice regimen described—five minutes every other day—acts as a continuous reinforcement learning loop, iteratively reducing the loss function associated with both temporal variance and spatial breaches.
